## The patch nobody thought twice about

Your systems administrator stops by with what he clearly expects to be a thirty-second
conversation. The vendor for Lakeshore's reagent and supply inventory-tracking system — the
tool satellite sites use to log lot numbers, expiration dates, and remaining stock for
collection-bag kits, test tubes, and the other consumables every draw depends on — has shipped
a routine security patch. Nothing about the patch touches how the software calculates anything;
it closes a login vulnerability flagged in the vendor's release notes. "I'll push it Thursday
night," he says. "Standard change, low risk, I'll note it in the change log same as always."

Normally you'd wave it through. This time you stop him. "Walk me through what 'low risk' means
here. What does this system actually drive?"

He talks it through out loud, and you can see him catch it mid-sentence: the inventory system
is where a site lead checks remaining shelf life before pulling a kit for a collection. If the
patch breaks a report, degrades a search function, or changes how an expiration date renders —
even temporarily, even for a few hours — a site could pull expired stock without anyone
noticing, because nobody else is cross-checking by hand anymore. That's not a service-impact
question. That's a product-quality question wearing an IT patch's clothes.

"Write it up as a change," you tell him — the same instinct your Quality Analyst (QA) has
heard from you before, about a different system, for the same underlying reason. "Not a
patch-and-note. A change."

## Why this matters — and the two bridges you already own

Here's the failure mode a casual "standard change, I'll note it in the log" approach risks: a
patch that looks purely technical turns out to touch something that affects whether a
regulated process still works correctly — and because nobody treated it as that kind of
change, nobody who actually understands the regulated side ever looked at it before it shipped.
The risk isn't that the patch is bad. It's that the question "does this affect anything
quality-relevant" never got asked by anyone with the authority to answer it, which is precisely
the gap `quality-system-essentials`'s own change-control module built its entire process to
close.

You already have a name for the discipline that's supposed to prevent exactly this: **change
enablement** — the ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) practice you've run for
years. Assess a proposed change's risk and impact, get it authorized by the right governing
body — usually a **CAB** (change advisory board), a cross-functional group that reviews and
approves changes before they ship — schedule and implement it, then review the outcome
afterward with a post-implementation review (PIR). That's the whole shape of what you just
walked your systems administrator through, in the vocabulary you've always used for it.

There's a second practice sitting right behind this one, and it's worth naming now because this
lesson builds both crosswalks together. Suppose that patch had shipped without this
conversation, and three weeks later the same login timeout starts recurring — not every day,
just often enough that the help desk has quietly reset the same three site accounts five times
without anyone asking why. That's **problem management**: investigating the root cause behind
a recurring or significant incident, logging a **known-error record** — the problem, a
workaround, and its root cause, kept in a **KEDB** (known error database) — when a permanent
fix isn't immediately available, and tracking toward that permanent fix. You already run this
discipline too, constantly, without thinking of it as anything exotic.

This lesson's entire job is showing you something you don't yet have language for: both of
these ITIL practices already have a direct, working counterpart inside Lakeshore's own quality
system, built and locked in `quality-system-essentials`. Change enablement maps onto
**change control**. Problem management maps onto **CAPA** (corrective and preventive action).
Neither mapping is a coincidence, and neither is exact. The job here is building both crosswalks
concretely enough that you can use them in a real conversation with your CIO (chief information
officer) or your exec quality council — not just gesture at "these are kind of similar."

## Crosswalk 1: change enablement ↔ change control

`change-control-for-regulated-systems` built Lakeshore's own five-stage process in detail:
**change request → impact and risk assessment → approval → implementation → verification.**
Line it up against change enablement's four moves, stage for stage.

| ITIL: change enablement | Lakeshore: change control | What's the same | What's genuinely different |
|---|---|---|---|
| Request for change (RFC) — what's changing, why | **Change request** | Both demand a documented trigger and scope before anything else happens. A request that can't state its own scope in a sentence isn't ready to move. | None worth naming here — this stage is close to identical in both worlds. |
| Risk and impact assessment — what does this touch, how likely and severe is getting it wrong | **Impact and risk assessment** | Both apply a likelihood/severity framework to the proposed change itself, not just the system it runs on. Both ask who else needs to weigh in before approval. | Lakeshore's assessment adds a question your normal CAB criteria were never built to ask: *does this change put a controlled process, document, or system out of a compliant, working state* — a question that can come back "yes" even when ordinary service-risk scoring reads low, exactly what the inventory-system patch surfaced above. |
| Authorization by a CAB (or a defined approver for lower-risk changes) | **Approval** | Both require a named approver with real authority to say no, not a rubber stamp after the decision is already made. | This is the honest difference, and it's worth stating plainly rather than softening it. A CAB is a cross-functional *body* — in principle, a majority of voices on that board could approve something one dissenting member objects to. Lakeshore's regulated change control doesn't work that way: **Quality is a required approver, not a notified party, and not one vote among several.** If Quality doesn't sign, the change doesn't go — there's no outvoting a Quality objection the way a CAB could, in principle, outvote a single dissenter. It's the same gate, narrowed and reshaped by regulation: fewer people can say yes, and one of them has veto power the rest don't share. |
| Implementation, on a scheduled release | **Implementation** | Both treat "shipped" as a milestone, not the finish line. | Lakeshore's version adds a completion condition a normal IT change doesn't carry: anyone whose work depends on the change — a site lead, collection staff — has to actually receive and understand what changed *before* the change's effective date, not learn about it from the deploy. |
| Post-implementation review (PIR) | **Verification** | Both exist to check the change actually worked, after the fact, instead of assuming a clean deployment means success. | Lakeshore's verification has to produce dated evidence the change achieved its intended, quality-relevant effect — not just "deployed without errors," which is implementation evidence standing in for verification evidence, the same substitution that module's own common traps section names directly. |

Run the inventory-system patch through both columns side by side, and the difference stops
being abstract.

**Under plain change enablement**, this patch is almost a non-event: low service risk, a short
RFC, probably pre-approved as a standard change by your normal criteria, pushed Thursday night,
reviewed at the next change meeting if anyone remembers to mention it.

**Under Lakeshore's change control**, the same patch becomes: a change request naming the
system and the specific fix; an impact assessment that explicitly asks whether the patch could
affect expiration-date display, search, or reporting — the actual quality-relevant function —
and names Quality and site operations leadership as consulted parties, because the system
touches lot tracking for materials used in collection; approval from Quality as the owner of
the process this system supports, and from you or your delegate as the owner of the system
itself — both real, both dated, neither standing in for the other; implementation timed so that
no site is mid-shift on an unverified version with nobody aware a patch just went in; and
verification that confirms, with evidence, that expiration-date logic, search, and reporting
still behave correctly post-patch — not merely that the login vulnerability closed.

Notice what didn't change: the shape is the same five-to-four-stage motion, assess-before-you-
approve, review-after-you-ship. What changed is who gets to say no, and what "done" requires
before anyone calls it done. That's the honest crosswalk — not "they're the same process," and
not "they're unrelated," but "same discipline, narrower gate, stricter finish line," the exact
pattern this curriculum has already used for other cross-framework comparisons elsewhere (a
Required safeguard under HIPAA and an Addressable one aren't the same promise, even though both
live under the word "safeguard"; Part 11's electronic-signature controls don't bend the way a
risk-based judgment call can). Don't flatten this one into "basically identical." It isn't, and
saying so honestly is the actual skill this lesson is teaching.

## A note on citations: there isn't a new one here

Nothing above introduces a regulatory source. `change-control-for-regulated-systems` already
grounded its five-stage process in 21 CFR 606.100(b) — the requirement that written procedures
be established, maintained, and kept available where they're used — and in AABB's (Association
for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) Process Control QSE, which supplies the actual
request-assess-approve-implement-verify structure Part 606's text never spells out. Go back to
that module for the citation decoder and the verbatim text; this lesson doesn't re-quote either,
and doesn't need to. ITIL's own side of the table is never cited to a specific publication
anywhere in this curriculum — it's used throughout as your own professional vocabulary, not a
standard requiring sourcing. Keep that distinction straight when you brief your CIO: the QSE
column above rests on regulation and an AABB standard; the ITIL column rests on nothing you'd
ever need to cite, because nobody's auditing Lakeshore's ITIL fluency.

## Crosswalk 2: problem management ↔ CAPA

Here's the second scenario, unrelated to the patch above. For months, the help desk has logged
a recurring ticket from one satellite site: staff repeatedly get locked out of the inventory
system mid-shift, usually twice a week, always resolved the same way — a password reset, a
"you're back in," ticket closed. Nobody has asked why this keeps happening at that one site and
nowhere else. Your QA notices the pattern first, because it reminds her of something she's seen
in a CAPA file: an action that keeps "working" without ever actually fixing anything.

**Under plain problem management**, this is a textbook known error. The incidents are the
symptom; the underlying cause hasn't been fixed, and a workaround exists — reset the password,
move on. ITIL's practice would have you log a known-error record: the problem (recurring
lockouts at this one site), the workaround (password reset), and a stated root cause once
someone investigates it, tracked in the KEDB until a permanent fix ships. That's a real,
legitimate practice, and it's exactly the discipline that keeps a known gap from just
disappearing into a pile of closed tickets that all look resolved.

**Under CAPA**, the same recurring failure has to clear a higher bar before anyone's allowed to
call it handled. `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness` built the four-stage structure this maps
onto: **root cause analysis** (pushed past the first "why," not stopping at a description of
behavior in the moment), a **corrective action** (fixes the instance in front of you), a
**preventive action** (addresses the systemic cause so it can't resurface elsewhere), and a
required **effectiveness check** — with its own measurable criterion, time window, data source,
and pre-agreed definition of failure, written down before anyone checks, not decided afterward
depending on what the data shows.

Run the lockout problem through both structures side by side.

| ITIL: problem management | CAPA | What's the same | What's genuinely different |
|---|---|---|---|
| Investigate the recurring incident's root cause | **Root cause analysis** | Both demand more than "it happened again" — a real investigation, not a description of the symptom. Pushing past "staff keep mistyping their password" to something systemic (say: a session-timeout setting at that site's network segment logs users out mid-shift, and the lockout threshold then treats the stale session's retry as a failed login) is the identical discipline either framework expects. | Neither framework differs here in what good practice looks like — a lazy problem record ("root cause: user error, workaround: reset password") fails problem management's own standard just as badly as it fails CAPA's. |
| Known-error record: the problem, workaround, and root cause, logged and tracked | **Corrective action** (fixes the instance) **+ preventive action** (fixes the systemic cause) | Both insist the workaround isn't the end of the story — a known-error record exists precisely so the organization doesn't forget there's still a permanent fix owed. CAPA's corrective/preventive split does the same job in two explicit pieces: patch the immediate pain (reset affected accounts, document the fix for this site) and fix the setting causing it everywhere it could exist (check every site's session-timeout configuration, not just the one that complained loudest). | None sharp enough to call a real difference — this is the strongest point of overlap in the whole crosswalk. |
| Track toward a permanent fix, workaround documented in the meantime | **Effectiveness check**: a measurable criterion, a time window, a data source, a pre-agreed failure definition | Both exist to stop a known gap from simply sitting there, tolerated indefinitely under a comfortable label. | This is the honest, real difference, and it's worth being precise about it rather than overstating it. A known-error record can, in principle, document a workaround indefinitely — ITIL's own practice doesn't set a hard requirement that the workaround ever gets retired, only that it stays logged and visible while a permanent fix is pursued. CAPA doesn't get to stop there. It stays open until someone checks, on a schedule set in advance, with real data, whether the failure mode actually stopped — and a CAPA "closed" the same week a fix ships, with no effectiveness data in the file, reads to an assessor as never actually verified, only completed. CAPA sets a stricter, more final standard of "actually fixed," not just "tracked." |

A concrete effectiveness check for the lockout fix looks like this, matching the same four
required pieces module 3 of `quality-system-essentials` built in depth: **criterion** — zero
recurring lockout tickets from that site's inventory-system users over a defined period;
**window** — the next 60 days; **data source** — the help-desk ticket log, pulled by someone
other than whoever implemented the fix; **failure definition**, agreed in advance — even one
recurrence in that window means the fix didn't address the real root cause, and the problem
gets reopened and investigated further, not quietly re-patched and left alone.

Here's the piece worth saying to your CIO in plain terms: a known-error record that never
closes isn't automatically a failure in ITIL's own world — tracked and visible beats silent and
forgotten, and that's a real, legitimate bar. It would be a failure in a CAPA file, because
AABB's framework doesn't treat "we're tracking it" as equivalent to "we proved it's fixed."
That's not ITIL being sloppy. It's two frameworks built for different stakes setting different
finish lines, and the regulated one is the stricter of the two.

## What an assessor or your CIO would actually look for

Nobody auditing Lakeshore checks whether you call this process "change enablement" or "change
control," "problem management" or "CAPA." The vocabulary is yours to use however gets the point
across fastest in whatever room you're in. What an AABB assessor, or an FDA investigator reading
a change or CAPA file, actually checks is whether the *substance* survived translation: a
documented request tied to a real trigger; an impact assessment that asked the regulated
question, not just the service-risk one; Quality's own dated, real approval sitting in the
record, not a courtesy mention; implementation evidence distinct from verification evidence; and,
for a recurring failure, root cause analysis that went past the first "why," a preventive action
scoped to everywhere the cause could exist, and an effectiveness check with a criterion that was
written down before anyone looked at the results.

A record built entirely in ITIL vocabulary, with no visible Quality approval and no effectiveness
check, is not a translation problem — it's a sign the regulated version of the process never
actually ran. The crosswalk in this lesson is for *your* understanding, so you can move fluently
between your CIO's language and your exec quality council's. It is not a substitute vocabulary
you can use in the record itself in place of the elements AABB's framework actually requires.

## Common traps

**"Our CAB has a Quality Analyst on it, so that's basically the same as Quality approval."**
It isn't, and this is the single most important distinction in this entire lesson. A CAB is a
cross-functional body that reaches a collective decision — in principle, a QA's single dissenting
vote could be outvoted by the rest of the board. Lakeshore's change control doesn't work that
way: Quality's sign-off is a required, independent approval with the power to stop the change on
its own, not one seat at a table that could, in theory, overrule her. If your mental model treats
"a Quality Analyst sits in the room" as equivalent to "Quality approved it," you're one disputed
vote away from a change going live that Quality actually objected to — which an assessor reading
the approval record would catch immediately, because there'd be no documented Quality sign-off
to find.

**"We've got a known-error record open on this, so it's being handled."** A known-error record
proves the gap is visible and tracked. It doesn't prove anyone has committed to checking, on a
set schedule with pre-agreed criteria, whether the underlying cause is actually gone. If a
recurring failure touches a quality-relevant process — the way the lockout issue does, given
that it's blocking access to a system staff rely on to verify expiration dates — "it's a known
error" isn't a stopping point. It's the trigger to open a CAPA, with its own effectiveness check,
not a substitute for one.

## What this means for your job

- **Before you wave through any change your team calls "standard" or "low risk," ask the
  question your systems administrator had to answer out loud above: what does this system
  actually drive, and could getting it wrong put a controlled process out of a compliant
  state?** That question, not the service-risk score, is what decides whether this needs full
  change control.
- **Confirm Quality's approval exists in the record as an actual sign-off, every time — never
  accept "she's aware of it" or "she's on the CAB" as equivalent.** If you can't point to a dated
  approval with her name on it, it isn't there.
- **Watch for a known-error record that's quietly become permanent.** A workaround that's been
  "temporary" for six months, with no effectiveness check ever scheduled, is the moment to ask
  whether this should have become a CAPA already.
- **When you translate between your CIO and your exec quality council, use the crosswalk to move
  fast — but never let the translation itself stand in for the regulated record.** "This is change
  enablement with a Quality veto" is a sentence that helps your CIO understand the stakes in five
  seconds. It is not a document an assessor would accept in place of the actual change-control
  file.
- **Treat "root cause: human error" the same way in both worlds.** Whether it shows up in a
  problem record or a CAPA draft, it's the same tell: the investigation found where the failure
  surfaced, not why the system let it surface there. Push past it regardless of which vocabulary
  the person in front of you is using.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator says, "Our CAB already has someone from Quality on it, so our change process already satisfies Lakeshore's regulated change-control requirement." Is he right?

No, and the gap is worth naming precisely. A CAB is a cross-functional body that reaches a
collective decision — a Quality Analyst's seat on it is one voice among several, and in
principle the rest of the board could approve something she objected to. Lakeshore's actual
change-control process requires Quality's sign-off as a **named, independent, required
approval** — not a vote that could be outvoted. If the change record shows only a CAB decision
with no separate, dated Quality approval, an assessor would read that as a missing approval,
regardless of who happened to be sitting in the room.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A recurring incident has had an open known-error record, with a documented workaround, for the last eight months. Is that record doing its job under CAPA's own standard?

Not on its own. A known-error record satisfies ITIL's own practice by staying visible and
tracked — that's a real, legitimate bar in that world. CAPA's standard is stricter: it requires
a root cause analysis, corrective and preventive action, and a required effectiveness check
with a pre-agreed criterion and time window, checked by someone independent of whoever
implemented the fix. Eight months of an open workaround with no effectiveness check scheduled
anywhere is exactly the gap this lesson's second crosswalk names — tracked is not the same
promise as proven fixed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Does AABB or the FDA require Lakeshore to use ITIL vocabulary — change enablement, problem management, CAB, known-error record — anywhere in its change-control or CAPA records?

No. This is worth stating plainly, because it's easy to let a good crosswalk blur into "these
are basically interchangeable requirements." ITIL is never cited in this curriculum to a
specific AXELOS/PeopleCert publication or page, because it isn't a regulatory or accreditation
standard at all — it's your own professional vocabulary, useful for translating what's
happening to your CIO or your team, quickly. What's actually required — a documented change
request, impact and risk assessment, named approval with Quality's required sign-off,
implementation, and verification; or root cause analysis, corrective action, preventive action,
and a scheduled effectiveness check — comes from AABB's own Quality System Essentials and the
21 CFR Part 606 floor underneath them, built in full in `quality-system-essentials`. Use ITIL's
words all day in conversation. Never let them substitute for the actual elements an assessor
would look for in the record itself.
:::

## Where this goes next

Change and problem are the two ITIL practices every IT leader already reaches for daily, which
is exactly why they made the right place to start this crosswalk. The next module picks up the
ITSM (IT service management) concepts that sit one layer further out — a CMDB (configuration
management database) and a service catalog — and maps them onto AABB's own equipment and
validated-system inventory and Lakeshore's quality-system scope, using the eQMS (electronic
quality-management system) itself as the first real artifact this course builds and carries
forward.
